items.q: Mechanically, a prompt is:
options: A command the model must obey
The context the model continues from
A setting that changes the model's weights
items.explain: Your text joins the context window and the model continues it. That is why supplying specifics beats insisting.

items.q: Writing 'THIS IS CRITICAL, BE ACCURATE' mostly:
options: Does little — there is no accuracy dial to shout at
items.explain: Emphasis is not a lever. Supplying the real source or constraint changes the answer; insisting does not.

items.q: The four parts of a clear request are:
items.explain: Task says what to do, context supplies material, format sets shape, audience sets vocabulary and depth.

items.q: You keep getting essays when you wanted a short list. The missing part is:
items.explain: An unstated format gets filled with the most common shape. 'Six bullets, one line each' fixes it at once.

items.q: Describing a document instead of pasting it gets you:
options: An answer about an invented document matching your description
A request to attach the file
items.explain: Omitted details get filled with what is typical, so the reply addresses a document that never existed.

items.q: Which context do people most often forget to supply?
options: What they already tried and rejected, and why
items.explain: Without it, iteration circles back to variations of the rejected answer — nothing signalled it was rejected.

items.q: A colleague's medical note would help draft an HR letter. You should:
options: Paste it; the privacy policy covers it
Not paste it — it is not your data to share, and redaction usually suffices
Paste it, then ask the model to forget
items.explain: Someone else's personal data is not yours to disclose, and 'forgetting' is not something you can verify.

items.q: 'Make it more professional' underperforms because:
options: It is ambiguous, so the most common reading is applied rather than yours
items.explain: Adjectives compress unstated preference. One line of specimen output makes your reading explicit.

items.q: Which is a checkable constraint rather than a wish?
items.explain: You can glance at the output and know whether it complied, which makes the next correction specific.

items.q: Requesting a 'where this came from' column mainly helps because:
options: It prevents the model from inventing
It gives fabrications nowhere to hide, making output auditable
It forces a live web search
items.explain: Structure does not improve truthfulness; it improves your ability to detect untruth, which is the part you control.

items.q: The first answer is most usefully treated as:
options: A verdict on the tool's quality
Evidence of how your request was actually read
The ceiling of what is possible
items.explain: It reveals how your words landed on something with no access to your intent, showing which part of the brief was empty.

items.q: Replying only 'no, try again' tends to produce:
options: A variation on what you just rejected
items.explain: Nothing communicated what was wrong, so the next attempt comes from the same region as the last.

items.q: 'Are you sure?' is weak verification because:
options: Agreeable tuning means it often folds regardless of correctness
It switches to a smaller model
items.explain: Capitulation is near-independent of whether the original was right, so the apology carries no information.

items.q: The strongest correction to a wrong figure:
options: Gives the right value and its location, and asks which conclusions change
items.explain: A wrong number propagates into the reasoning; correcting the number alone leaves the conclusions quietly broken.

items.q: You have corrected the same error twice and it recurs. Best move:
options: Correct it a third time, more firmly
Ask it to promise not to repeat it
items.explain: The error persists in context as apparent fact. Firmness does not remove it; a fresh conversation does.

items.q: An unconnected assistant gives a specific figure for your firm's private revenue. That is:
items.explain: Specificity is not evidence of access. With no genuine connection to the source, confidence is the warning sign.

items.q: The core problem with 'is this contract safe to sign?' is:
options: Nobody is accountable when it is wrong and you cannot appeal
items.explain: Beyond accuracy, professional advice carries liability and recourse — much of what you actually pay for.

items.q: Converting an impossible request well means keeping:
options: The judgement with you, delegating the preparation
The judgement with the model, delegating facts
Both with the model, then verifying
items.explain: Asking which clauses to examine, or what to ask a lawyer, leaves the decision where accountability lives.

items.q: A prompt becomes a reusable template when you:
options: Replace the specifics with clearly marked slots
items.explain: Slots are what make it reusable — the reasoning stays fixed while the particulars change each time.

items.q: Keeping your prompt library in plain text you own matters because:
options: Tools change, and fair comparison needs a prompt neither vendor controls
items.explain: Portability survives feature and pricing changes, and is a precondition for the comparison method in E2·L10.

items.q: A template that reliably produces confident, unchecked output is:
options: Worse than no template, because it makes an error routine
items.explain: Automating an unverified step repeats the same mistake efficiently. Saved prompts should have verified output.

items.q: Asking a model 'why did you say that?' returns:
options: An audit trail of its processing
items.explain: It has no privileged view of its own workings. Treat such explanations as narration, not evidence.
